strengths: The austere coastal palette, botanical plates, literary serif typography and specimen-label details create an unusually specific identity for Marram.
The plant register is more than decoration: season bars, exposure notes and garden cross-references make the studio's expertise tangible and memorable.
The £450 first visit is consistently named, priced and explained, with well-positioned calls to action across long pages.
Mobile is deliberately recomposed: featured specimens gain scale, secondary cards become compact editorial rows, and garden summaries remain legible rather than merely collapsing.

defects.detail: Several plant records publish blank beige placeholders—most visibly Glaucium flavum, Echinops ritro and Achillea millefolium. In a site whose entire visual proposition depends on a curated botanical register, these read as broken or unfinished assets.
The missing plates undermine the otherwise meticulous archival presentation and make the planting catalogue feel incomplete at the precise point intended to prove specialist knowledge.
Desktop supporting copy, specimen metadata and seasonal labels are frequently very small and low-contrast, weakening comprehension and making important evidence feel incidental.
Some mobile specimen rows become crowded, with narrow text columns forcing awkward scientific-name wraps and clipped-looking content near the card boundary.

The primary action remains visible, but the long mobile register creates extended stretches without a conversion prompt; a contextual first-visit link between later groups would catch visitors once the evidence has persuaded them.

summary: This is distinctive, strategically aligned work with a strong editorial system and a convincing signature botanical-register moment. It falls short of pass because missing specimen artwork damages the central visual idea and professional credibility; completing those assets and refining small-text legibility would move it into strong design-team territory.
